1121.title: For the ways of peace (Gittin 61a)
1121.hook: the Talmud rules that poor non-Jews are fed and their sick visited, for the ways of peace
1121.howItsDone: Jewish food pantries, visiting committees and charities often serve neighbors of every background, and some cite the ruling 'for the ways of peace' as one reason.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the page is open: Beruriah reading closely, and a page of Talmud that asks only to be read. Today, a short phrase that widens a familiar list.

Feed the poor. Visit the sick. Bury the dead. Familiar duties, done by neighbors, by burial societies, by the person who brings soup. The Talmud takes that list and adds a few words that change its size. Not only for the Jewish poor, the Jewish sick, the Jewish dead. For non-Jews too, side by side with them. And it gives a reason in one short Hebrew phrase. Today's word is that reason.
screen: `FEED, VISIT, BURY.` → `NOT ONLY YOUR OWN.` → `SIDE BY SIDE.`

segments.voice: For the ways of peace. In Hebrew, mipnei darkhei shalom. First, the ruling. In tractate Gittin, the Talmud brings a teaching: the poor of non-Jews are supported along with the poor of Israel, their sick are visited along with the sick of Israel, and their dead are buried along with the dead of Israel, for the ways of peace. Along with. Not after. Not instead. Second, a phrase with a family. The Mishnah in the same tractate lists other rulings made for the ways of peace. The Torah reading in synagogue goes first to a priest, then a Levite, then any other Jew, so nobody quarrels over who goes first. And poor non-Jews are not stopped from gleaning in the fields. Small rules that keep a shared street calm. Third, the size of it. The Talmud goes further, and says the whole Torah is for the sake of the ways of peace. Its proof is a verse from Proverbs about wisdom and Torah: "Her ways are ways of pleasantness, and all her paths are peace." Fourth, two ways to hear it. Some readers hear the phrase as practical wisdom: neighbors who are cared for stay neighbors. Others, Maimonides among them, tie these rulings to a verse in the Psalms saying that God is good to all and has mercy on all his works, and to the Proverbs verse, as if to say the law is simply acting like its Giver. Both readings live in the tradition. Either way, the soup goes to every door on the street.
screen: `FEED, VISIT, BURY: ALONG WITH ISRAEL.` · `SMALL RULES FOR A SHARED STREET.` · `ALL HER PATHS ARE PEACE.` · `PRACTICAL WISDOM, OR GOD'S OWN WAY?` · then, large: `FOR THE WAYS OF PEACE.`

segments.voice: Picture your circle, family, friends, the people who share your faith or your table, and let your attention drift to its edge: a neighbor you only nod to, the person who delivers your packages, someone of another faith, or none. Let one face come forward, and hold it with goodwill for a few breaths.
For the ways of peace. Mipnei darkhei shalom: the Talmud's reason for feeding, visiting and burying non-Jews along with Jews. Today's word.

segments.voice: Your line: for the ways of peace. Along with, not after. Rest well.

1122.title: The hard passages
1122.hook: some passages are troubling; teachers and communities read them honestly, in context
1122.howItsDone: Jewish teachers and study partners often stop at a troubling passage to ask who is speaking, what the discussion is about, and how later commentators and codes treated it. Communities differ in how they explain and respond to such passages.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ways of peace: the poor, the sick and the dead of every people, cared for along with Israel. Your line: for the ways of peace. Today, the lines that are hard to read.

A sentence lifted off a page of Talmud can travel a long way. Sometimes it turns up online, cut loose from everything around it, offered as proof that the whole book is cruel. Sometimes a student meets one in class and goes quiet. The question underneath is real. The Talmud is a huge record of argument, and some of what its sages said is hard to read today: lines about women, about outsiders, about punishment. Careful teachers don't pretend those lines aren't there. What they do with them is today's lesson.
screen: `A SENTENCE CUT LOOSE.` → `SOME LINES ARE HARD TO READ.` → `WHAT TEACHERS DO WITH THEM.`

segments.voice: Read in context. Start with who is speaking. A page of Talmud is a conversation, so a line may be one sage's view, raised so the next sage can push against it. A view on the page isn't automatically a ruling. Then ask what the page is arguing about, and what came just before. Then ask what later law did with it: some statements were set aside, and some were read so narrowly they almost never applied. The Talmud shows this move itself, with one of the hardest laws in the Torah. Deuteronomy describes a stubborn and rebellious son, brought by his parents to the elders of the city. The sages read that passage so closely that a teaching in tractate Sanhedrin says such a son never was and never will be. Then why was it written? Study it, and receive reward. A hard verse becomes a reason to study, not a sentence to carry out. But context isn't an eraser. Some passages stay hard after all the explaining, and teachers who take the text seriously say so. Communities respond in different ways. Some read a hard line as belonging to its own time and place. Some search the commentators for the reading that guards a person's dignity. Some name the hurt plainly and keep studying beside it. What they share is a refusal of two shortcuts: hiding the passage, or waving it around without its page. Read the whole page first. Then judge it.
screen: `WHO IS SPEAKING?` · `WHAT IS THE PAGE ARGUING?` · `A SON WHO NEVER WAS.` · `CONTEXT IS NOT AN ERASER.` · then, large: `READ THE WHOLE PAGE.`

segments.voice: Choose a line that troubles you, from scripture or any book, and hold it in mind. Ask who is speaking, what came just before it, whom it might hurt, and whom it might have been meant to protect in its own day. Don't rush to fix it or throw it out; let it stay hard for a moment, and keep breathing beside it.
The hard passages. Lines in the Talmud that trouble readers today, which Jewish teachers read honestly, in context, without hiding them and without cutting them loose. Today's word.
Your line: read in context. A quotation without its page is only half a quotation. See you tomorrow.

1123.title: The Talmud laughs
1123.hook: puns, jokes and absurd cases fill its pages
1123.howItsDone: In yeshivas and study partnerships, learners often enjoy the Talmud's wordplay and its strange hypothetical cases, and teachers sometimes open a class with something light before turning to the text.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hard passages: read the whole page, and admit what stays hard. Your line: read in context. Today, the same book, laughing.

Before the lesson, a joke. Tractate Shabbat says that the sage Rabbah, before he began teaching, would say something funny, and his students would laugh. Then he would sit in awe and begin. A joke first, then the work. It's a small detail, and it says something about the book it sits in. A text this serious has room for laughing, and sometimes the laughter is part of the teaching.
screen: `RABBAH TELLS A JOKE.` → `THE STUDENTS LAUGH.` → `THEN, IN AWE, THE LESSON.`

segments.voice: The Talmud laughs in more than one way. There's wordplay. The prophet Isaiah promises that all your children will be taught of the Lord, and great will be their peace. The Hebrew for your children is banayikh. A teaching at the end of tractate Berakhot says: don't read it banayikh, your children. Read it bonayikh, your builders. The ones who learn become the builders of peace. One small change in sound, and the verse opens. Then there are the absurd cases, pushed to the edge to see where a rule breaks. The Mishnah says a young bird found within fifty cubits of a dovecote belongs to the dovecote's owner. Rabbi Yirmiyah asked: and if one foot is within fifty cubits and one foot is outside? The Talmud reports, completely deadpan, that for this question they put him out of the study house. Readers still differ about whether he was teasing or deadly serious, and whether the sages were annoyed or laughing too. And then there are the mice. In tractate Pesachim, a house has been searched for leaven before Passover. A mouse goes in with bread in its mouth. A mouse comes out with bread in its mouth. Same mouse? Same bread? The sages work it through with complete seriousness, and that's the comedy: great minds at full power, chasing a mouse. Why keep all this on the page? Partly because a sharp case sharpens a rule. Partly, like Rabbah's joke, because a laughing mind is an open one. On these pages, seriousness and laughter sit at the same table.

segments.voice: Bring back something that once made you laugh because it was clever: a pun, a riddle, a child's question that stumped the grownups. Let it be funny again, and notice where the smile starts. Then ask, lightly, what it taught you.
The Talmud laughs. Puns, absurd cases and a teacher's opening joke, kept on the same pages as the law, because a sharp case and an open mind both help learning. Today's word.

1124.title: The sages were human
1124.hook: the Talmud records its heroes' flaws and quarrels
1124.howItsDone: Students of the Talmud meet its sages' mistakes and quarrels in the text itself, and teachers often discuss what those stories teach about humility, compassion and repair.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the talmud laughs: a pun about builders, a bird on the line, a mouse with bread. Today, a hero's cold moment.

A calf is being led to slaughter. It breaks away, runs to a great rabbi, and hides its head in the folds of his robe, crying. The rabbi is Rabbi Judah the Prince, the sage tradition credits with editing the Mishnah. He looks down at the frightened animal and says: go. For this you were created. And he lets them take it away. The Talmud tells this about one of its own heroes, plainly, and it doesn't stop there.
screen: `A CALF RUNS TO THE RABBI.` → `GO. FOR THIS YOU WERE CREATED.` → `THE TALMUD TELLS IT ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: Tractate Bava Metzia tells it plainly. Because he showed no compassion, suffering came upon Rabbi Judah, and stayed with him for years. Then one day his maid was sweeping the house and came upon some young weasels, and began to sweep them out. He stopped her. Let them be, he said, and quoted the Psalm: "His tender mercies are over all His works." And the Talmud says that because he showed compassion, the suffering left him. Notice what the book has done. It could have polished him into a statue. Instead it shows a giant in a cold moment, the cost of that moment, and the small act that turned him. And it isn't a lone story. The Talmud also tells how Rabban Gamliel, the head of the sages, was removed from leadership after he publicly shamed a colleague. The heroes misjudge, wound each other and change, right there on the page, in front of every student who will ever open it. Why would a tradition tell its children that their heroes failed? One answer: if the sages were perfect, nobody could follow them. A flawless teacher leaves you nothing to do but admire. A teacher who failed and turned leaves you a path. And the teaching keeps going past the teacher's flaw. Rabbi Judah's Mishnah is still studied, and so is the story of the calf and the weasels, side by side.
screen: `THE CALF HIDES IN HIS ROBE.` · `THE WEASELS: LET THEM BE.` · `HEROES WHO FAIL ON THE PAGE.` · `A FLAWED TEACHER LEAVES A PATH.` · then, large: `HIS TENDER MERCIES ARE OVER ALL HIS WORKS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you look up to, and let one of their real flaws come into view. Don't defend them, and don't throw them away; hold both at once, what you admire and where they fell short. Then, gently, let one of your own flaws stand beside theirs.
The sages were human. The Talmud keeps its heroes' cold moments, quarrels and turnings on the page, so students can follow them, not only admire them. Today's word.
Your line: the sages were human. A flaw can be followed by a turning. Until tomorrow.

1125.title: Where is my partner? (Bava Metzia 84a)
1125.hook: Resh Lakish, once a gladiator, becomes Rabbi Yochanan's study partner; after he dies, Yochanan can't be consoled
1125.howItsDone: In yeshivas and study programs, learners often study in pairs, and the story of Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish is told to show what a true study partner means.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sages were human: a calf in a rabbi's robe, and weasels he let be. Today, two partners and a quarrel.

A question about knives. When does a blade count as a finished tool: when it comes out of the furnace, or when it's plunged into water? It's a dry point of purity law, the kind the study house argued over. Two old partners are arguing it. Rabbi Yochanan, the great teacher. And Resh Lakish, the rough man from the riverbank whom Rabbi Yochanan drew into a life of study; another tractate says he had once sold himself to the arena. On this ordinary question, one sentence is about to break them apart.
screen: `A QUESTION ABOUT KNIVES.` → `TWO OLD PARTNERS.` → `ONE SENTENCE.`

segments.voice: Tractate Bava Metzia tells it. Rabbi Yochanan says the blade is finished when it leaves the furnace. Resh Lakish says when it's quenched in water. And Rabbi Yochanan answers: a robber knows his trade. A jab at his partner's old life. Resh Lakish answers, stung: what good did you ever do me? There, among the robbers, they called me master. Here, they call me master. Rabbi Yochanan replies: I brought you near, under the wings of the Divine Presence. Both are wounded. The story says Resh Lakish fell ill. His wife, Rabbi Yochanan's own sister, came weeping and begged her brother to pray for him, for her children's sake. He answered her with a verse from Jeremiah, about God caring for the orphan and the widow, and he did not relent. Resh Lakish died. And then the great teacher fell apart. You may remember the next part: the sages sent him a brilliant student who only ever agreed with him, and it didn't help. Rabbi Yochanan tore his clothes and wept, crying out: where are you, son of Lakish? Where are you? The Talmud says he cried until his mind gave way, and the sages prayed for mercy for him, and he died. It's a hard page, and the tradition kept it whole. It doesn't say who was right about the knives. It says what a partner is worth: the person who argues with you until things come clear. And it measures that worth the hard way, by the empty chair.
screen: `A ROBBER KNOWS HIS TRADE.` · `HE DOES NOT RELENT.` · `WHERE ARE YOU, SON OF LAKISH?` · `MEASURED BY THE EMPTY CHAIR.` · then, large: `WHERE IS MY PARTNER?`

1126.title: After the oven (Bava Metzia 59b)
1126.hook: Rabbi Eliezer is shut out after the argument, and the story warns about wounding words
1126.howItsDone: The laws against wronging with words (ona'at devarim) are studied as part of Jewish ethics and law, and the story of Rabbi Eliezer and Imma Shalom is often taught alongside them as a warning about how the winners treat the one who lost.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rabbi Yochanan's cry for Resh Lakish. Your line: where is my partner. Today, another argument, and what came after it.

The argument is over. Over a clay oven, the sages have outvoted Rabbi Eliezer, turned away a carob tree, a stream, leaning walls and even a voice from heaven, and declared: it is not in heaven. The majority has won. The Talmud could close the story there. It doesn't. It turns instead to the one who lost: Rabbi Eliezer, put under a ban, sitting outside the circle he once taught in. And then it turns to his household, and to one woman who saw what that loss had done.
screen: `THE MAJORITY HAS WON.` → `THE ONE WHO LOST.` → `A WOMAN WHO SAW IT.`

segments.voice: Start with where the story sits. The oven isn't in a chapter about ovens. It sits in a chapter of Bava Metzia about ona'ah, wronging. The pages around it are about wronging with words. Don't remind someone who has turned their life around of what they used to do. Don't ask a seller the price of something you have no intention of buying. And the sages say that one who shames another in public, so the color drains from their face, is like one who sheds blood. Then comes the oven. Then its aftermath, told through Imma Shalom. She was Rabbi Eliezer's wife, and her brother was Rabban Gamliel, the head of the sages who had banned her husband. She knew what her husband carried. So, the story says, she kept him from falling on his face in the private prayer of supplication, afraid of what his pain might bring down. One day she was distracted, and found him with his face to the ground. Get up, she said; you've killed my brother. A horn sounded from Rabban Gamliel's house: he had died. How did you know? her husband asked. She answered with a tradition from her father's house: all the gates may be locked, except the gates for one who has been wronged. The cry of the one who was hurt goes straight up. That's the warning the page leaves. Winning an argument is allowed; it's how the law moves forward. But the person on the losing side still has a face, and that gate stays open.
screen: `A CHAPTER ABOUT WRONGING.` · `SHAMING IS LIKE SHEDDING BLOOD.` · `IMMA SHALOM KEEPS WATCH.` · `THE GATE THAT STAYS OPEN.` · then, large: `WORDS WOUND.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who lost recently, an argument, a vote, a job, a place in the group; maybe you were on the winning side. See their face as it is now, not as it was in the fight, and let their disappointment be real to you. Then think of one word that would give them back their dignity.
After the oven. The part of the story after the argument is won: the one who lost, the hurt he carried, and the gate that stays open for the wronged. Today's word.
Your line: words wound. Even when the argument was yours to win. Go gently.

1127.title: The one who left (Chagigah 15a)
1127.hook: Elisha ben Abuya left the tradition, yet his student Rabbi Meir kept walking and learning with him
1127.howItsDone: The story of Elisha ben Abuya and Rabbi Meir is studied in Chagigah and often discussed in Jewish teaching about how to treat people who have left the tradition.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the gate that stays open for the wronged. Your line: words wound. This week, the Talmud showed its human face; today, a sage who left.

A horse on the road, and a man in the saddle, on a day when Shabbat law doesn't allow riding. Walking behind him, on foot, is one of the great teachers of the Mishnah, listening, asking questions, learning Torah from the rider. The rider was once his teacher, a sage who has since left the tradition. The walker is Rabbi Meir. And at a certain point on the road, the rider pulls up and tells his student to turn back. Today's word is the name the rabbis gave the rider.
screen: `A RIDER ON SHABBAT.` → `A STUDENT WALKING BEHIND.` → `TURN BACK.`

segments.voice: Acher. The other one. His name was Elisha ben Abuya, a great sage who, in the Talmud's telling, broke from the tradition he had taught. The rabbis stopped using his name and called him Acher, the other. Tractate Chagigah tells what his student did next. Rabbi Meir didn't stop learning from him. On that Shabbat, Acher rode and Meir walked behind, the two of them trading verses and readings as they went. Then Acher said: Meir, turn back. I've been counting my horse's steps, and here is the Shabbat limit. Beyond this point you may not walk. Look at that. The man who has left still guards his student's Shabbat, and still knows the law down to the step. And Meir answers him: you, too, turn back. Come home. Acher says he can't. He says he heard a voice from behind the heavenly curtain, repeating the prophet's call, "Return, ye backsliding children", and adding: all except Acher. So they part at the boundary, one turning back toward the town, one riding on. The Talmud doesn't tidy this up. It doesn't say Meir was wrong to walk with him, and it doesn't say Acher came back. It shows a student who refused to let his teacher's leaving end the conversation. Readers differ about what Meir was doing on that road: learning, hoping, loving, or all three. The text keeps the picture. Two people on one road, one on a horse and one on foot, still talking, right up to the line.
screen: `ACHER: THE OTHER ONE.` · `THE STUDENT WALKS BEHIND.` · `HERE IS THE SHABBAT LIMIT.` · `ALL EXCEPT ACHER.` · then, large: `STILL TALKING, UP TO THE LINE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who walked away from something you share: a faith, a family tradition, a team, a circle of friends. You don't have to agree with where they went; just notice whether the two of you have stopped talking. Then picture walking a little way beside them, still talking.
Acher. Hebrew for the other one: the name the rabbis gave Elisha ben Abuya after he left, the teacher his student Rabbi Meir kept walking with. Today's word.
Your line: he kept walking with him. His leaving didn't end the conversation between them. Rest well.
